== Biography ==
{{African-American Sticker}}
{{Heritage Sticker|ancestors=Native American}}
{{Occupation |image=Black_Heritage_Sticker_Images-5.png|text=was a blacksmith.}}

Isaac C. Glasko was born ca. 1776, and died on September 2, 1861.   He was the son of [[Glasko-5 | Jacob Glasko]] and Matilda (Unknown).

A native of Rhode Island, he settled with his family in North Uxbridge, Massachusetts by 1790, where he became a blacksmith and, in 1806, purchased land with his brother George Glasko from Alexander Stewart in Griswold, Connecticut.  The land was along the Pachaug River, according to Preston land records bounded by a dam and an old Iron works; the transaction included the right to open the dam and to divert water for use in his blacksmithing business. 

He received, in 1807, a third of the 50 acres that his father had acquired in Griswold, Connecticut.

He continued to work as a blacksmith in Griswold, Connecticut, constructing a water-powered trip hammer forge.  He initially produced tools for local farmers and later tools for the shipping and whaling industries.  Very successful, his business grew to 10 employees.

In 1823, with his friend, Pero Moodey, he petitioned the Connecticut General Assembly for an exemption from taxation, arguing that, because they were unable to vote, they should not be required to pay taxes.  The petition was read to a select committee, but the legislature rejected the petition.

In 1841, in declining health and with some financial issues, he sold off land to satisfy his debts.

He was a respected member of the community and the town of Glasgo is named in his honor.
 
His surname appears with  number of variations in the public records: Glasko, Glasco, Glassko,, Glassgo, Glassgow, Glasse, Glasgo. 

Isaac Glasko was born around 1776 in Cumberland, Rhode Island to Jacob Glasko and Lucy Brayton Glasko.  He was of both Native American and African American Heritage. He married Lucy Brayton of Smithfield. <ref name="Griswold">[https://www.griswold-ct.org/about_our_town/index.php#:~:text=Tool%20Inventor%20Isaac%20Glasko%2C%20a,name%20now%20known%20as%20Glasgo. === History ===
The village of Glasgo in  Griswold, Connecticut is named for Isaac Glasko.  The misspelling is due to a post office clerical error. <ref name="Griswold"/>

By 1800 he and  his wife had relocated to North Uxbridge, Massachusetts in the Blackstone Valley. His father Jacob and brother George followed him and also moved  to the Blackstone Valley. <ref name="PhillipsWar"/> 

In 1806 Isaac, his father and brother moved to Griswold Connecticut. Isaac purchased from Alexander Stewart (also a member of the Kinne family) three-quarters of an acre  of land and a house, along with the rights to water-power access from the dam where Stewart had a grist-mill. That same year, Jacob Glasko (still of Massachusetts) purchased fifty acres of land and a house along the Pachaug  River and by the edge of a pond (now Glasgo Pond) for $1,250, a third of which holdings  he sold to each of his sons in 1807. <ref name="BurialGrounds"/>

Issac established a business as a blacksmith and grew it into a commercial forge  employing  as many as  10 blacksmiths manufacturer producing farming implements as well as harpoons for the whaling industry, among other things. His blacksmith shop was constructed near the what is now the intersection of Route 165 and Route 201. He harnessed waterpower to a large mechanical trip hammer  that sped the manufacturing process and enabled him to make large tools. <ref name="Griswold"/><ref name="ConnHistory"/>

The Glaskos were  active in buying and selling land in the area. Isaac owned 54 acres.  By 1841, he owned at least 54 acres of land with four dwelling houses, a sawmill, a gristmill, two barns, a coal house, and a number of other small outbuildings. <ref name="BurialGrounds"/>

Isaac Glasko and his friend Pero Moody (1750-1830) filed a petition in 1823 to teh Connecticut General Assembly requesting exemption from taxation on the grounds that they could not vote. In part, the petition states that they were "descendants of African Citizens brought to this County against their will" and that "in the midst of most mortifying discouragement have  acquired some property"  <ref>Rejected  Bills,  Connecticut State Legislature, Records Group  002, Box 2, Folder 3).</ref> <ref name="BurialGrounds"/> <ref name="ConnHistory">[https://connecticuthistory.org/blacksmith-isaac-glasko-challenges-the-state-constitution/ Connecticut History Blacksmith Isaac Glasko Challenges the State Constitution]</ref>

 Isaac's daughter, Eliza Glasko attended Prudence Crandall's academy for young ladies in Canterbury from 1833-34, which is  thought  to be one of the first integrated schools.<ref name="Griswold"/>

 His house still stands, although it has been considerably altered.  Isaac Glasko final resting place with his  wife are in a quiet burying ground near the center of the village that now bears his name now known as Glasgo.<ref name="Griswold"/>

== Research Notes ==
=== Individual father review, 22 October 2026 ===

This dated review supersedes any earlier grade of this pair within the stated record scope. The existing father [[Glasko-5]] is assessed at 88% (probable). The held Isaac biography explicitly names Jacob and Matilda, describes the family’s Rhode Island–Uxbridge–Griswold movement, and records Isaac receiving a third of his father’s land in 1807. That specific family and property narrative supports Jacob substantially beyond a surname-only attachment.

Derivative historical account; the original 1807 conveyance and its kinship wording are uninspected.

Next useful test: Read the 1807 distribution and identify its grantor and grantees.

Source basis already held: [https://www.google.com/books/edition/After_King_Philip_s_War/LXrgK29zl2QC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Isaac+Glasko&pg=PT344&printsec=frontcover After King Philip's War: Presence and Persistence in Indian New England edited by Colin G. Calloway (https://www.google.com/books/edition/After_King_Philip_s_War/LXrgK29zl2QC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=Isaac+Glasko&pg=PT344&printsec=frontcover)]. No new original inspected; no new father attached.
